summary:
Pahang stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" and acts of "gross indecency", carrying up to 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. The offences turn on the conduct rather than on gender or consent, so they reach visitors as well as citizens.

Every Malaysian state and the federal territories maintain Sharia enactments that criminalise cross-dressing or "a man posing as a woman", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those offences reach Muslims only. A non-Muslim foreign visitor in Pahang is therefore exposed to the Penal Code and not to the state Sharia layer.

No legal gender-recognition procedure is recorded for Malaysia, and no federal law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. A visitor whose documents do not match their presentation has no statutory protection against being challenged on that basis.

Enforcement across the country concentrates on venues and queues rather than on private conduct. Police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur on 28 November 2025 and arrested 208 men under section 377B; detainees' faces and personal details were published, more than 130 people were held at one point, and 31 foreign nationals were among them until their embassies intervened. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed.

Since the 2018 election the documented pattern has been public and raid-based: at least 20 LGBT people were arrested in an October 2022 raid on a Queer Halloween party in Kuala Lumpur, twenty men were arrested in an August raid on an LGBT venue, and a Terengganu Sharia court ordered a lesbian couple caned. In November 2023 Johor announced plans for conversion-therapy centres.

Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters interviewed 73 LGBT people across Malaysia between 2018 and 2021, and Pahang was among the states where interviewees lived. The report records no enforcement case specific to Pahang. It also records that government-run "rehabilitation" programmes had drawn at least 1,733 attendees by June 2021.

For a visitor in Pahang the operative exposure is the federal Penal Code, not a local operation: no Pahang-specific raid, prosecution or arrest is documented in these sources. Discrimination and violence against LGBT people are regularly reported nationally, and transgender people are identified as particularly vulnerable.
tangentialFactors:
Litigation has narrowed the state Sharia layer without loosening the federal one. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, while Penal Code offences remained fully intact; a High Court had earlier refused to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional.

Trans people in Malaysia face lethal violence. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in fewer than two months, and documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity.

Official hostility is on record. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister said the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department had his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked; in the Nur Sajat case 122 religious officers were mobilised before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection.

Reform prospects are constrained by Islamist opposition, LGBT events and media content are censored, and there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law. Government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats and the June 2021 attendance figure of 1,733 place Pahang residents inside a national programme of that kind.
localsOnly:
Residents of Pahang who are Muslim are subject to the state Sharia enactment layer as well as the federal Penal Code, with cross-dressing offences carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Enforcement of those provisions is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and the enactments contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.

Residents also face the federal provisions in full: sections 377A and 377B apply regardless of gender or consent, and there is no legal gender-recognition procedure through which a resident can align official documents with lived gender.

With no statute prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, residents have no domestic legal recourse in employment, housing or public services. Pahang residents interviewed for the 2018-2021 Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters research described national-level conversion practices, discrimination and violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Pahang-specific enforcement case appears in the source inventory. Whether Pahang's own Sharia enactment uses the national three-year, RM5,000, six-stroke scale, and whether it also bars women from posing as men, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

Whether Pahang operates government-run "rehabilitation" programmes, or has hosted mukhayyam retreats, is not stated in these sources and is unresolved.

The inventory does not record any venue-style raid in Pahang equivalent to the November 2025 Chow Kit operation, nor any prosecution under sections 377A or 377B originating in Pahang. Absence of such a record in these sources is not evidence that none has occurred.

Pahang's local rules on venues, raids or police powers of stop and search are not covered by the supplied sources and remain unresolved.
